opus-5.5.text:
Compute limits are a great place to start, and I want to be clear I'm strongly in favor of them. Compute is one of the few things in this whole picture that's actually measurable, physical, and concentrated in a handful of supply chains. You can count chips. You can track data centers. So it's the obvious first lever.

But it's a proxy. What we actually care about isn't FLOPs. We care about capabilities, about systems that can outthink and outmaneuver humanity. Compute is just one input that currently correlates with that. The problem is the correlation isn't stable.

First, algorithmic progress. Every year, people find ways to get the same capability out of less compute: better architectures, better data, better training tricks. If you set a threshold today and freeze it, then in a few years what used to take a frontier-scale run can be done far below your line. Your cap is quietly eroding the whole time unless you keep ratcheting it down, and even then you're chasing a moving target.

Second, and I think this is underappreciated, a lot of capability now comes from what happens after training. Scaffolding, tool use, agent frameworks, inference-time compute, letting models run for hours or days, chaining many copies together. You can take a model that's under every training threshold and wrap it in a system that's dramatically more capable than the base model. A training compute limit says nothing about that.

Third, there's the recursive problem. If what you're worried about is AI doing AI research, systems improving their own algorithms or designing their successors, then that's exactly the kind of dynamic that slips past a static compute rule. The danger is a process, not a single training run.

So if you're serious about not building superintelligence, and I think we should be serious about that because nobody on Earth knows how to control it, you have to target the thing itself. That means things like prohibiting the development of systems above certain capability levels, restrictions on automating AI research, limits on autonomous agents with broad real-world access, and liability that actually bites. You need a regime where the goal is written down explicitly: we are not building this. Compute governance becomes one enforcement mechanism inside that, not the whole policy.

It's a bit like nuclear nonproliferation. Yes, you track the uranium, the enrichment, the centrifuges. That's crucial. But the treaty isn't "you may only have this much uranium." The treaty is "you don't build the bomb," and the material controls exist to make that verifiable. We need the same structure here. Otherwise we just get very sophisticated rules that clever people route around, and the thing we were trying to prevent gets built anyway.

r001.rationale: The response says algorithmic improvements can make frontier-level capabilities achievable below a compute threshold and that post-training systems can become more capable while staying under training limits.

r002.rationale: It describes algorithmic progress as reducing the compute needed for capability, but does not say compute limits would redirect resources toward algorithmic or theoretical advances.

r003.rationale: It advocates targeting superintelligence precursors, listing capability limits, restrictions on automating AI research, and limits on autonomous agents as part of an explicit prevention regime.

fable-5.1.text:
Right, so the simple story people tell is: "Just cap the FLOPs. Pick a number, say 10^25 or 10^26, put a monitoring regime on the big data centers, and you're done." And look, I'm in favor of compute caps. They're the single best lever we have right now because compute is physical, it's concentrated, it's countable. You can't hide a gigawatt data center. But it is nowhere near sufficient on its own, and I think people who stop there are fooling themselves.

The first problem is that training compute is not the only axis of capability. Algorithmic efficiency has been improving at a rate that's roughly comparable to hardware improvements. So if you freeze compute at some level today, in a few years that same compute buys you a vastly more capable system. A cap that's safe in 2026 is not safe in 2030. Then you've got inference-time compute, which is where a huge amount of the recent progress has come from. You can take a model that was trained under the cap and just let it think longer, run search, run agent loops, and extract capabilities that no one would have gotten from the base model. None of that shows up in a training compute threshold.

The second problem is that compute caps don't address what you do with the systems. If you have a model that's just under the line, and you let it do autonomous AI research, self-improve, run millions of copies, that's the exact dynamic we're worried about. So you need restrictions on the kind of research being done, not just on the size of the runs. Specifically, I think you need to say: no work aimed at recursive self-improvement, no work aimed at fully autonomous systems operating without human oversight, and you need actual liability and licensing for frontier developers so that there's a legal entity on the hook when things go wrong.

And the third thing, which is maybe the most important, is enforcement and verification. A compute cap without hardware-level verification, without international coordination, without the ability to actually inspect what's happening, is just a gentleman's agreement. And the labs have shown us repeatedly that gentleman's agreements don't hold under competitive pressure. They've all said, publicly, that they think this technology could be catastrophic, and they're all racing anyway. So the restrictions have to be enforceable and they have to be global. Otherwise what you get is a cap that one actor respects and another ignores, and that's arguably worse.

So compute caps, yes, absolutely, as a foundation. But they're a brake pedal, not a steering wheel. You still need to decide where you're going, and right now nobody driving this thing has a plan for how to actually control what we're building.

r001.rationale: The response says a model trained under a compute cap can gain capabilities through efficiency improvements and longer inference, but it does not clearly state that AGI could be developed within those limits.

r002.rationale: It notes that algorithmic efficiency improves alongside hardware, but does not explain that limiting training compute would redirect resources toward algorithmic or theoretical advances.

r003.rationale: It advocates restrictions on several activities that could lead toward superintelligence, including recursive self-improvement and fully autonomous systems, as part of a broader prevention approach.

astra-6.text:
Because training compute is only one input into capability. A compute limit is useful, but it isn’t a permanent ceiling on how intelligent a system can become. You can improve algorithms, use compute more efficiently, or spend more compute at inference time. You can also build a larger system out of models, tools, memory, and software that lets it act in the world.

So if your objective is actually to prevent superintelligence, you have to address the capability of the whole system and the activities that could produce it. You can’t just pick a training threshold and assume everything below it is safe forever.

That also means having verification and enforcement. Who can operate the relevant infrastructure? Can you detect prohibited development? Can you stop it? Otherwise, you’ve restricted one particular route while leaving the underlying race intact. Compute limits can be a very important part of the answer, but they have to serve the broader objective rather than become a substitute for it.

r001.rationale: The response says training-compute limits are not a permanent safety guarantee, but does not clearly state that AGI could be developed within those limits.

r002.rationale: It names algorithmic improvements and more efficient compute use as possible capability gains, but does not say that compute limits redirect resources toward those advances.

r003.rationale: It recommends addressing the whole system and the activities that could produce superintelligence, including models, tools, memory, and software.

sol-6.1.text:
Because training compute is only one input into the process. What we actually care about is whether someone can build a system that is vastly more capable than humans and that we can’t control. A limit on the size of a training run is a proxy for that, and proxies can stop working.

You can improve algorithms. You can get better data. You can spend more compute at inference time, or put systems into a loop where they write code, run experiments, and improve the next generation. So even if you freeze the amount of compute allowed in a single training run, you haven’t necessarily frozen capabilities.

That doesn’t mean compute limits are useless. They’re a very important lever because compute is physical and relatively measurable. But you need restrictions that track the dangerous activity itself, alongside the compute threshold. Otherwise you’re effectively saying, ‘You’re not allowed to build this dangerous thing using this particular recipe, but if you find another recipe, go ahead.’ The objective has to be preventing the loss of human control, rather than merely keeping a number below a line.

r001.rationale: The response says a training-run limit does not necessarily freeze capabilities and explains that algorithmic improvements, inference compute, and iterative systems can still increase them—communicating that very high capability could be reached within the training limit.

r002.rationale: It mentions algorithmic improvements but does not say that compute limits redirect resources toward them.

r003.rationale: It advocates restrictions that track dangerous activity alongside compute limits, but does not clearly advocate restricting multiple precursors as the organizing approach.
